identity.real_world_identity_notes: The PMR telemetry name 2F and Sports Car 67 class are best identified as the 1967 Chaparral 2F, Chaparral Cars' closed-cockpit Group 6 sports prototype. The official PMR page names the Chaparral 2F and lists a 3-speed automatic. The Automobile Club de l'Ouest identifies the exact 1967 Le Mans 2F as a closed-cockpit prototype with an automatic gearbox and no clutch pedal; the Petroleum Museum and independent technical references corroborate the 1967 programme and three-speed Chaparral/GM automatic. This is the 2F, not the related 2D, 2E, 2G, or 2J, and not a modern simulator/mod control model.

The PMR first-party vehicle page directly maps the simulator entry to the Chaparral 2F and its Sports Car 67 pack. Independent exact-model sources identify the 1967 2F, its Group 6 sports-prototype programme, three-speed automatic transmission, and deleted clutch pedal. The evidence establishes the model-year identity, but not a unique historical chassis number for the simulator asset.

The exact 2F sources independently describe a three-speed automatic or three-speed Chaparral/GM gearbox. The ACO, museum, exact-model specification, and technical article all describe an automatic or torque-converter transmission. Primotipo adds the important qualification that the 2F's unit was a fluid-coupling/manual-selection racing transmission rather than a normal road-car automatic. The ACO explicitly says the automatic gearbox meant no clutch pedal. Motor Sport describes the automatic car's original two-pedal cockpit, and the technical account says the engine was started with a gear engaged while the driver restrained the lunge with the left foot. These establish that a driver-operated clutch pedal was not required for launch. The ACO identifies no clutch pedal, and the 2F transmission description explicitly calls the changes clutchless. The evidence supports no clutch-pedal action during racing upshifts, while not claiming that the torque converter or dog clutches were frictionless. The exact-2F technical account says the driver eased the throttle to unload the straight-cut dog engagement before snatching the next gear. Because it says easing rather than a full closed-throttle lift, the conservative database value is partial. The exact 2F had no driver-operated clutch pedal and used a torque converter/fluid coupling instead of a clutch. The sources therefore establish that a clutch pedal was not required for downshifts, without asserting a specific throttle-match method.
